issues.legal_issue: A claim to enforce rights arising from a property purchase in the name of a person’s wife or unmarried daughter is not barred by the prohibition on suits and defences concerning benami property.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued to obtain relief concerning properties he alleged he had purchased in his wife’s name.
The defendant sought rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was barred by Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988.
The Supreme Court held that the suit could proceed, while leaving the plaintiff to prove his claim at trial.
issues.conclusion: Section 4(1) and (2) does not prohibit a suit or defence concerning either a present or past purchase made by a person in the name of his wife or unmarried daughter. The order rejecting the application to strike the plaint was upheld, and the suit was remitted for disposal according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(a) defines a benami transaction, while Section 3(2) permits a purchase in the name of a wife or unmarried daughter notwithstanding the general prohibition in Section 3(1). Reading Sections 3(2), 4(1) and (2), and 5 together, the Court held that permitting the purchase but preventing enforcement of rights arising from it would be contradictory; the exemption would also be rendered redundant if the transaction were subject to the consequences applicable to prohibited transactions. The Court noted R. Rajagopal Reddy v. F. Chandrasekharan, which held that Section 4 applies prospectively, and the earlier contrary view in Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare; it held that Section 4 bars neither present nor past purchases of this permitted kind. The distinct exceptions in Section 4(3) were not the basis of this holding.

predicates.benami_rights_enforcement_case: A person brought a suit or raised a defence to enforce an asserted right concerning property acquired through a transaction in which one person provided consideration and another held title.
predicates.purchase_in_wife_or_unmarried_daughter_n: A person acquired property in the name of that person’s wife or unmarried daughter.

issues.definition: When a person seeks to enforce rights concerning a transaction in which the property was acquired in that person’s wife’s or unmarried daughter’s name, the claim is not barred on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A person seeking to enforce rights concerning a purchase in the name of a wife or unmarried daughter must prove that the purchase was not for her benefit.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed that properties titled in his wife’s name had been purchased by him for his own benefit.
The plaintiff’s suit had not yet been decided on its merits when the defendant sought rejection of the plaint.

The Court held that the plaintiff could obtain relief only by proving that the properties had not been purchased for his wife’s benefit, even if he proved that he had provided the purchase consideration.
issues.conclusion: The statutory presumption is that a purchase in the name of a wife or unmarried daughter was for her benefit unless the contrary is proved. The claimant must rebut that presumption to obtain relief; proof that the claimant paid the consideration alone does not suffice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 provides that, unless the contrary is proved, property purchased by a person in the name of that person’s wife or unmarried daughter is presumed to have been purchased for her benefit. A claimant seeking relief must prove the contrary, even if the claimant establishes that the consideration came from the claimant.

predicates.claimant_seeks_rights_in_property: A claimant seeks to establish a right to property acquired in the name of another person.

issues.definition: In a claim concerning property acquired in a person’s wife’s or unmarried daughter’s name, the claimant must prove that the purchase was not for her benefit.
